canonical_concept.beeja: गुं (Guṃ) — the bīja associated with the Guru principle in Tantric traditions.
canonical_concept.vyakarana: Guru is an adjective (meaning "heavy, weighty, important") used as a noun. It is also used as a title. The feminine form is Gurū or Gurviṇī. The word is used in both the sense of "teacher" and "heavy/important."
canonical_concept.functional_meaning: The Guru is the teacher who transmits knowledge (vidyā) from the tradition to the student. In the Vedic tradition, knowledge cannot be obtained from books alone — it must be transmitted from Guru to student in an unbroken lineage (paramparā). The Guru removes the student's ignorance (avidyā) and guides them toward liberation (mokṣa). The Guru-śiṣya (teacher-student) relationship is the foundational relationship of Indian civilization.
canonical_concept.dhatu: गृ (Gṛ) — To swallow, to take in; also connected to गुर् (Gur) — heavy, weighty. The guru is the "heavy one" — weighty with knowledge.
canonical_concept.nirukta: "Gu-kāraś cāndhakārasya ru-kāras tannirodhakṛt" — Gu represents darkness (ignorance), Ru represents its removal. The Guru is one who removes the darkness of ignorance. This etymology appears in the Advayatāraka Upaniṣad.
related_concepts: samskara (upanayana — the saṃskāra of entering the guru's household)
canonical_concept.tattva: Guru-Tattva — the principle of the teacher who transmits knowledge and removes ignorance. In Kashmir Śaivism: Guru-tattva is one of the thirty-six tattvas — the principle of divine grace operating through the human teacher.

claims.value: In Advaita Vedānta: the Guru is the external manifestation of the inner Guru (Ātman). The Guru's teaching points the student to their own true nature. In Tantra: the Guru is the living embodiment of the divine — "Guru is Brahma, Guru is Viṣṇu, Guru is Maheśvara" (Guru Gītā). In Kashmir Śaivism: the Guru is the agent of Śiva's grace — śakti-pāta operates through the Guru.

claims.value: In Purāṇic cosmology: Bṛhaspati is the Guru of the gods (deva-guru); Śukra is the Guru of the demons (asura-guru). The concept of Ādi-Guru (the first Guru) — Śiva is the Ādi-Guru who taught yoga to Pārvatī. The concept of Guru-paramparā (lineage of teachers) — the unbroken chain from the divine source to the present teacher.

The concept of guru-kṛpā (Guru's grace) — the transformative power of the Guru's attention and blessing.

claims.value: The concept of Guru in governance: the rāja-guru (royal teacher) was the king's spiritual and political advisor. Cāṇakya (Kauṭilya) was the paradigmatic rāja-guru — he guided Candragupta Maurya to establish the Maurya Empire. The concept of dharma-guru (teacher of righteousness) — the Guru who guides the ruler in dharmic governance.

pipeline.value: The Guru is the teacher who transmits knowledge (vidyā) from the tradition to the student. In the Vedic tradition, knowledge cannot be obtained from books alone — it must be transmitted from Guru to student in an unbroken lineage (paramparā). The Guru removes the student's ignorance (avidyā) and guides them toward liberation (mokṣa). The Guru-śiṣya (teacher-student) relationship is the foundational relationship of Indian civilization.
